utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. There is still one matter pending, Mr. Thayer. These are the documents you have tendered so far. Most of them have been received, but from your list, the last part of it, the fourth part, there are some matters open. We have received P992 because this is clearly related to our witness, Mr. Kingori. It is his OTP statement. But we have not made any decision about P993, 994, 995, 996, and 997. If I'm not mistaken, I got an information but through the Registry from the OTP that they have a different record. I don't know how you will proceed, Mr. Thayer. If there is no showing that there is any relation between this witness and these documents and you haven't used them, I don't see the basis for tendering and admitting them. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, good morning to you and Your Honours. The relation to the witness is simply that these documents were either shown to the witness in his prior testimony by various parties. I believe mostly by Defence counsel during his cross-examination. I think there may have been one or two that were shown in redirect examination by the Prosecution. So they were used, shown, to the witness last time around. As I said yesterday, the only thinking behind including them on the list of exhibits was to assist Your Honours in making sense of the Popovic trial transcript as you reviewed it so that you could literally see in front of you what the witness was seeing at the time. Otherwise you'll have no access to these documents. Again, for example, there were some video stills which were shown by one of the Defence teams to the witness. They are not that clear but I figured I'd give Your Honours the opportunity to at least see what the witness saw so that you can make your assessments of the testimony. So that's the connection to the witness that we saw and that was the thinking behind including these. Again, if Your Honours don't feel the need to have these exhibits to assist Your Honours, that's fine, but that was the reason we put all these documents on there because they were used with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, but this is the difference: They were used but not tendered and not admitted into evidence. And to have that in evidence in our trial, there is a need to show it to the witness, to deal with that with the witness. For instance, the OTP statements with two other witnesses, I don't see any purpose of tendering them with this witness. You may do that with the other witnesses if they will be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. We are not clamoring to put Mr. Nuhanovic's statement before the Trial Chamber, it's not something that we feel an independent need to, as far as I know. So that is perfectly fine. Perhaps -- and we've gone -- I think we've gone back and forth on this suggestion in the past, but it may be a solution to simply MFI these documents in the event that the Trial Chamber feels the need to go back and look at them. They are not in evidence. The Prosecution will not be seeking to otherwise use them, but they will be available for the Court's review. That may be an intermediate solution. If that doesn't please the Court, then we'll just proceed as, Mr. President, you've suggested and maybe they will surface at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will mark them for identification, but I'm not sure why you didn't use the diary of this witness with this witness during examination-in-chief, P996.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The reason, Mr. President, was it wasn't used by the Prosecution in the last case. Frankly, the diary surfaced in the middle of his examination. Just to give you a brief background, he testified in December of 2008. We learned during his proofing that he had in fact managed to smuggle out one of a few notebooks that he had kept at the time. However, that was back in Nairobi, if I remember. So he had to return to Nairobi over the recess. He brought the diary back with him. We made it available to Defence counsel. They used it during their cross-examination to some degree. We didn't feel it necessary to re-open our examination-in-chief or to add additional examination based on the diary. So we -- the Prosecution didn't use it, but it was used by Defence counsel. And I didn't see any need to affirmatively use it before this Trial Chamber. I think the contents of the diary are perfectly consistent with what he has already testified about. The extent to which the Defence used it is in the record, but again, I thought it might be helpful to have the hard copy available for the Court to review if Defence counsel, for example, is reading from it or has read a portion, but the -- or, for example, if the witness has read certain portions to himself on the record, if it doesn't come in, then nobody knows what anybody is talking about. You'll have the page reference, perhaps, but not the actual text. So theoretically, Mr. President, what we could do is somehow use all these documents so that we have a connection here before this Trial Chamber, but I didn't think that would be productive. So that's my thinking on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, the Chamber is of the view that these documents can only be admitted into evidence if they are tendered through the current witness. These documents not related to a prior and received transcript of a statement or testimony in another case. Mr. Tolimir, do you want to respond? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. As far as the statement of Hasan Nuhanovic goes, we really cannot see any great link with the testimony of this witness in the Popovic case. But as far as the other documents are concerned we have no objection whatsoever, especially P995. It is a part of the report on Srebrenica of the Dutch Institute for War Documentation. That is a document which is both relevant and the information contained in it was used in the cross-examination of this witness, although it may not have been tendered in the Popovic case. As far as the notebook of this witness is concerned, we would just like to see this notebook in the Serbian language as soon as possible so I could convey the contents, summarise it to Mr. Tolimir. Since we had no time to review this notebook, it was written in longhand in English and it's not so easily legible, we think that one should be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that it is not possible to receive them, the documents P993 through P997 into evidence because they were not used with this witness and not admitted in a prior trial either. The documents P995 and 996 have no translation yet. They couldn't be received but they are all already marked for identification with the given numbers. So this the decision of the Chamber. The documents may be used with another witness or by the Defence, it's to the parties. Now, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down. Welcome back to the courtroom. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth that you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. Sorry for the delay, we had to discuss a procedural matter. Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let me greet all those present. I wish peace unto this house. May this day and this whole trial be completed in keeping with God's will, not necessarily mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Witness. I would appreciate it if we could continue. Before we embark upon a new area of questioning, I'd like to go back to that question that remained open yesterday about Tuzla as a protected area, because it was contested here that it was a protected area. On page 5382, lines 22 and 23, you said that Tuzla was not a protected area of the United Nations and the Prosecutor said the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show 65 ter 1980, which is the UN Security Council resolution of May 1993. We will look just at the operative part of this resolution. We haven't got it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just noticed that it's not uploaded in e-court under this number. It's 1D286. That's the number under which it was uploaded. For the record, the same document is on the Prosecutor's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 2 of this resolution, could it please be shown. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Recalling the provisions of Resolution 815 of 1993 on the mandate of UNPROFOR and in that context acting under Chapter 7 of the charter, item 3 says: "Declares that the capital city of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo, and other such threatened areas, in particular the towns of Tuzla, Zepa, Gorazde, Bihac, as well as Srebrenica, and their surroundings should be treated as safe areas by all the parties concerned and should be free from armed attacks and from any other hostile act." Now item 4 says: "Further declares that in these safe areas the following should be observed: "A, the immediate cessation of armed attacks or any hostile act against these safe areas, and the withdrawal of all Bosnian Serb military or paramilitary units from these towns to a distance where from they cease to constitute a menace to the security and the inhabitants of these towns to be monitored by the United Nations military observers." It will also be relevant for our discussion to look at paragraph 6, which says: "Requests the Secretary-General to take appropriate measures with a view to monitoring the humanitarian situation in the safe areas, and to that end, authorises the strengthening of UNPROFOR by an additional 50 United Nations military observers, together with related equipment and logistical support and in that connection also demands from all parties and others concerned to co-operate fully and promptly with UNPROFOR." Now, based on what I've just read I'd like to ask you, could you tell us, on this basis, did the Security Council with its Resolution 824 recall that Tuzla was also a UN protected area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what you've said, Your Honour, I think it declared Tuzla a UN protected area. What I had said earlier is that personally I did not -- I had not included Tuzla in the safe areas during my statement that I gave. I did not indicate Tuzla. And that has been the contention, but that does not mean that Tuzla was not a UN protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. We see from this that in these areas there were varying regimes of work, both on the part of the military observers and the balance of powers in Sarajevo, Tuzla, Bihac, and protected areas Srebrenica and Zepa and Gorazde. There was a variety of mandates; is that true or did everyone have the same mission?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't understand the question because the mission of the UN was the same except in the UN protected areas, which was different from the other areas of former Yugoslavia. And also the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will rephrase my question to try to make it clearer. Did a military observer in Srebrenica and Zepa have the same mission as the military observer in Tuzla, Bihac, Gorazde, or Sarajevo? We are talking about the mission carried out on the ground, not the mandate.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are talking about the mission, it was the same for military observers who were in UN safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In Srebrenica, in addition to all the other tasks that other missions elsewhere performed, did you also have the additional task of ensuring that the area is indeed militarised, because other teams did not have this demilitarisation component?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I went there in that enclave, that is, Srebrenica, the mission was the same as has -- had always been before and even thereafter in now -- the other protected areas, that is. On the side of demilitarisation, it had already been done, and let's get it very clearly that demilitarisation by the time we arrived there had already been done. All the heavy weapons had been removed from the Muslims and taken to a safe area. That is the same with all the other enclaves. By the time we arrived there in 1994, 1995, all that had been done, so there's nothing new that we were going to do. We were not going there to demilitarise that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please, when you see that my microphone is on, let me ask you an additional question. Were there any weapons in other areas, Sarajevo, Bihac, Gorazde, Tuzla, like there were weapons in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Were the weapons removed in other areas such as Sarajevo, Bihac, Gorazde, and Tuzla, like they were removed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I request that we specifically go to Srebrenica. If the question is concerning Srebrenica, I will tell that you the weapons had been removed and taken to Bravo Company, where they were stored. In other areas, I don't know where they had been taken to, except maybe Sector East where I can tell that you they had been put in various locations, not one location. But in Srebrenica it was in one location, that is Bravo Company, where they had been taken to. So maybe other observers will tell you where the weapons were kept in those other safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please assist the Trial Chamber and tell them whether a zone is demilitarised if only heavy artillery is removed whereas all the rest remains in use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand your question, but when you say some who are in use --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer the question directly. You can say whatever but we need an answer.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, demilitarisation was a removal of the weapons from the locals. And that was done. That was done and they were moved to the -- to the Bravo Company and we found them there, and we could see them. We could count them. We had a list of all the heavy weapons which were there. But as I said yesterday, if you're talking about a comparison between the arming of the Bosnian Serb army and the Muslims really is of no comparison. There were small arms here and there but that does not mean that there were not demilitarised --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, I didn't ask you that. I asked you whether -- please, could you answer my question, if you remember what I asked you and then you can say whatever you wish after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, I think this is not appropriate, what you are doing with the witness at the moment. You are putting questions and I think we all have the obligation to listen to the answer. You shouldn't interrupt him so many times, and he is providing you with an answer as is he able to do that. Listen to the answer. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday in the course of one hour I managed to put only six questions. If that's the way he goes on answering today, I can immediately tell you that I will no longer cross-examine. I have over a hundred questions left. I asked the witness whether demilitarisation means that only heavy artillery is removed. Can he please answer me first and then he can go on talking about other things, and according to your instructions, I will not interrupt him again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I agree with you. Sometimes some witnesses have a very lengthy answer, but every witness does it in a different way, like the Prosecution and the Defence put some lengthy questions to witnesses. On the other hand, I think the witness has answered your question several times already what in his understanding demilitarisation means in these so-called safe areas. The last question again, Mr. Kingori, related to heavy weapons, but before you answer, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just note a couple of things briefly. First, these questions were asked yesterday, exactly the same questions, and Colonel Kingori provided a very detailed answer to the best of his ability. If General Tolimir doesn't like the answers, then he can ask a different question, but to threaten the proceedings with taking his ball and going home and not further cross-examining witnesses because, frankly, he is asking repetitive questions is not helpful to this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, not really for the witness, just to clarify the current dialogue. If you go to page 10 of today's transcript, line 1, the question -- line 4, the witness said in answer to the question from General Tolimir: "... demilitarisation was a removal of the weapons from the locals. And that was done." I think that, to me, is an answer to your question, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you focus on the key of your questioning, please carry on, but be patient with the witness, please. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And thanks go to the Prosecutor and the witness. I will not have any sub-questions. I can only ask the witness whether all the weapons were taken from the Muslims in Srebrenica. He was an observer. He was there. I will respect his answer. I give him the floor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it forces me to repeat the same answer that I gave yesterday, that the removal of the heavy weapons was done and even the other weapons was done, but then you could not be able to ensure that all small arms, all pistols, AK-47s were removed from the locals in Srebrenica itself. So that really does not -- if you compare with the weaponry that the Bosnian Serb army had, really, there's no comparison. So you cannot compare with the arming with the small arms that the Bosnian Serbs had -- the Muslims had and the heavy weapons that the Bosnian Serb army had. Here, as I said yesterday, they had the tanks, they had the heavy artillery, they had the mortars, the rocket-launchers, and all those heavy weapons. When we talk about artillery, artillery we are talking about the heavy ones, the 155 millimetres, et cetera. And those were heavy weapons. It was also an organised army, a conventional army, that is the Bosnian Serb army, as compared to what we had in the enclave, there was nothing. So concerning the small arms fire that we may have had, and because we noted it in the situational reports that occasionally we could hear some small arms fire, there are times that we could see some of the Muslims inside there with small arms is in our reports. But that does not compare with what the Bosnian Serbs army had at all. It does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was an answer that we have received yesterday already. That is very clear. And Mr. Tolimir, to make the best use of the time available for you and everybody else in the courtroom, please try not to repeat a question which is already answered. That's all I what want to say. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, we did not hear the following question: Did the UN forces and military observers have to ensure the parity of weapons of the Serbs around Srebrenica and the Muslims in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the demilitarisation agreement, is there a single provision according to which the Serbs were supposed to either surrender or reduce their weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they were supposed to do, that is, the Bosnian Serb army, was to refrain from attacking the UN protected areas. That is one thing that I know. And they had to remove their weapons from an aggressive posture, a posture that threatens the people who are living in the enclave. That is, they had to remove them from positions close by the enclave to ensure that the people inside the enclave feel safe and not threatened. This did not happen because they still positioned themselves in attacking positions in areas that we have already put in our situation reports where we had the rocket-launchers, the anti-aircraft guns and also the artillery weapons which were actually facing the enclave. This was a threatening posture.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please can you answer my question again because you didn't answer. If you cannot remember my question, I'll repeat it. In the demilitarisation agreement, was there a single provision pursuant to which the Serbian army had to reduce the parity of their weapons in the area around the enclave of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, you said before the Trial Chamber that you had undergone training before you went to Srebrenica and that training took place in Zagreb. Did you learn during that training that the demilitarised zone was being armed again by means of helicopters and in other ways? Did you learn that the Muslims were being armed yet again? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not learn that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in Srebrenica as a military observer, did you see a single command military structure in Srebrenica, and did you inspect any such structures and did you introduce yourself to them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can say is that there was no conventional military or army in the Muslim side. It was not there. The fact that they had someone they could call a Chief of Staff or an intelligence officer does not necessarily mean that they had a conventional army. You can imagine, you know, some -- the opposing side, that is the Bosnian Serb army, they had all the way up to generals. In the enclave itself, that is the Muslim side, as far as I am concerned, they had no such rankings, and if they had, really, where would you position an army in Srebrenica itself? An army, and you know very well because, Your Honour, you are an army general, so at least you know, an army is composed of three divisions minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each division is composed of three brigades as a minimum. Each brigade is composed of three units and all the supporting arms. Each unit is composed of three companies. Really, in such a small enclave where would you hold all that? So it was not an organised army. And it was a rag-tag, you know, if we can call it that, it was something that was not organised at all. But compare it with the Bosnian Serb side. They had everything, they had all the support weapons, they had the infantry itself, and it was a complete army with the proper structure. We did not see that proper structure in the Muslim side at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a military observer, did you receive a task to reduce the Army of Republika Srpska to the level of the command structure that existed in Srebrenica, or perhaps not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have such a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the Chief of Staff and the security organ, did they exist at all despite the fact that the Muslims did not have a proper army, as you have just explained?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope you are asking the Chief of Staff, he was there. There was a Chief of Staff, Ramiz Becirovic. He was the Chief of Staff for the Muslim side. And as for the issue that you talked about concerning the reduction of the army on the other side, that is on the Bosnian side, really it was not in our mandate. I just want to elaborate slightly further. It was not in our mandate to reduce. But it was in our mandate to ensure that we observe the violations to the cease-fire agreement, you know, atrocities that may be committed from either side. And mainly the ones who had the more advanced weaponry, you know, here we are talking about the ones -- the Bosnian Serb side are the ones who were in a more aggressive position. So we had to hold meetings from -- you know, with both sides to ensure that at least we would bring these people to an understanding and that we reduce the suffering of the people in the enclave because as far as the UN was concerned, this was a protected area and the people therein had to be protected from aggression from outside. From outside, here I mean from the Bosnian side army -- Bosnian Serb army. So that was in our mandate and we had to ensure that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since that was your mandate, can you finally answer me this: Did you meet with that fictitious Chief of Staff of whom you said that he existed and the security organ when you arrived in the protected zone? After you've answered me that, we can continue talking about other things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've even mentioned his name. I met him and I've even mentioned his name, Ramiz Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I quoted from the resolution that the number of observers was increased by 50 in the protected areas despite the presence of UNPROFOR. Can you tell me what the difference was between your role, the role of protecting the areas, as you said it, and the role of UNPROFOR? What was the difference between your two mandates?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained, and I think I explained yesterday, the role of the UN military observers, so I think the best thing now I will explain the role of UNPROFOR, if you didn't get it yesterday. UNPROFOR were armed. These were battalions and they were armed and they had to protect the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Really, Mr. President, I think the witness was interrupted mid-answer. If he had finished, then I'll sit down, but I think he was literally in the middle of a sentence before he was cut off by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think he was at the beginning of his answer. You were asking for the difference between the -- between UNPROFOR and the role of the observers. The witness wanted to explain that related to your answer. You should listen to him. Please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The military -- the UNPROFOR were armed battalions which were sent to the former Yugoslavia with the aim of doing their mandate as given by the United Nations Security Council. They were to protect those people who were inside there, but the mandate in some cases actually did not allow them to use force. I think there are two different mandates, but at least one thing we can note, they had a proper structure of -- from the commanding officer all the way down to the lowest level, that is the section. And they manned the observation post, they manned the surrounding areas, and they ensured that there is peace inside the former Yugoslavia. Different UN detachments, that is different battalions, were given different areas to man. Like we had several, I think there were about ten or so battalions from all over the world, including a Kenyan battalion which was there somewhere in Knin. But if you go back to the military observers, these were senior officers ranking from major and above and sometimes you could get some captains who were there to observe the VCFAs, that is a variation to the cease-fire agreement, and report. They were not living in the normal barracks. They were living together with the locals so that they can be able it to integrate with them, know how they operate, and know their culture, and ensure that they are free to give them any information that can help bring the warring factions together. They were also there to ensure that they bring -- they get -- they hold meetings with both factions so that they can understand the problems which are facing them and so that they can be able to convey whatever they are told from this side to this other side to bring the warring factions to a better understanding and maybe even end of the war. Another reason why the military observers were not armed was to ensure that they are safe in that they could not be attacked because they don't have any weapons. We could hear of attacks on the battalions but on the military observers, it was very rare, very rare. It happened, but very rare, because these people were not armed and they were free to move anywhere. Another point to note is that the military observers, though unarmed, used to provide protection even to some of the battalions against the aggressors. They could be able to provide security for the UNHCR, the IOM, and all those other organisations when they are moving from one point to the other because it was known that the report from the UN military observers was stronger than even the others from the quarters. It was stronger because it was based on facts, not hearsay. It was based on facts, and before you write something you had to make sure that you are writing the truth because it would involve a lot of other issues and it was taken very seriously all the way up to the UN Security Council. So, basically that is the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your explanation. Could you please tell us whether you UNMOs had a book of rules which you had to follow in your work, and did it differ from the book of rules that UNPROFOR and other structures present in the protected area of Srebrenica had to observe and work by? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said it before but I will still say it again, that we were different. We had a different structures, even administratively. We had different reporting systems. Sometimes we could be able to compare notes, but mainly our structures were different. For the observers it started from the team, that is the observer team. Like team Srebrenica, we could report to our senior military observer who was in headquarter Sector North-east and it would go to the chief military observer in Zagreb. This was different from the UNPROFOR side. UNPROFOR had their own structures and they had to go all the way to the general who was the commander of the UN peacekeeping force in Bosnia -- in former Yugoslavia. We were different. We had different reporting systems. The work system was different and we knew it and understood it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And was there a book of rules for the observer mission Mr. Tolimir was asking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But was there a book of rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you have one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had our own regulations and rules to follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- which were different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us this: How did your regulations regulate your work as UNMOs in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica, and could you also please tell us what -- what was the name of the regulation that you had to follow, that book of rules? Did it have a title, did it have a name, and if it did, could you tell us the name of that regulation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't remember the name of those regulations, but we had ours which were different from those of the UNPROFOR. And even the work that we were doing was different, other than for some areas where we -- you know, they were coinciding. You know, some areas we had to consult each other. But our work was very different from the work of the UNPROFOR. Secondly, the regulations that governed the UN military observers, as I've said earlier, was very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for having asked you this again. I didn't know that you had regulations and that's why I asked you what was the title of your book of rules. In addition to UNMO -- in addition to regular tasks that UNMOs had and that are described in the regulations, did UNMOs also have to supervise the implementation of agreements if such an agreement was signed by the warring parties in an area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I've already answered that when I said we were to ensure the observance and that the violations to the cease-fire agreement were not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will remember your answers if your answers are shorter. In order to help me not to repeat myself, try to help me and provide more succinct answers. I apologise for the repetitions and I'm kindly asking you tell me whether in Srebrenica there was a cease-fire agreement that was assigned by the warring parties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a cease-fire agreement that had to be observed in the whole of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the cease-fire agreement, was there any other agreement that you got to review when you came to take up your duties as UNMO in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not go there to review any cease-fire agreement. That was not in our mandate, and that is your question, and we did not go there to review any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you now about the demilitarisation agreement, not the cease-fire agreement. Was there a demilitarisation agreement that was in place at the time when you were there, and did anyone show that agreement to you or any other UNMO?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the cease-fire agreement was also composed of the demilitarisation in the UN protected areas. It was all encompassing, but if we put the emphasis more on the UN protected areas, those inside the enclaves were to be disarmed and their arms -- I'm actually repeating what I had said earlier. Their arms put in a safe area, but the ones outside, and still giving an example of Srebrenica, we are talking about the Bosnian Serbs army, they were to refrain from posturing in an attacking mode in a way that would threaten the safety of those inside the enclave. They were also to refrain from attacking them at all. And that is why the UNPROFOR -- that is the UN protection through an army battalion was ensured. It was already in the enclave to ensure that that does not happen. And that is for the same reason that the military observers were put inside there to ensure that these, if it happens, is reported immediately to the UN system so that they can be able to do something themselves as a UN system. So at least the UN had already taken care of that, that is it's protected and there are systems to ensure that if violations are done, it's reported immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell me if you have ever seen an agreement on demilitarisation between the Muslims in Srebrenica and the Serbs around Srebrenica, or between the Bosnian Serbs army, as you call it, the VRS, and the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it's not coming out clearly or we are not understanding each other during the question and answer sequence, but if I can just tell you we had the cease-fire agreement and that is what I'm emphasising on. This is the one that also had the demilitarisation bit of all the UN safe areas, all the UN protected areas. It was encompassed in that cease-fire agreement. So if you are directing the question to show like if there was an agreement between the Muslims and the Bosnian Serb army, I don't remember seeing anything like that, that they themselves had agreed other than what was agreed as their cease-fire agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since when you were giving your statement you attached a great number of documents including your diaries, did you also attach this cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to make it clear for the record, when the witness -- and I don't think there's any dispute from the Defence on this. When the witness gave his OTP witness statement in 1997, which I presume is what General Tolimir is referring to here, he did not have the diary or was not asked for it. So that was not, as I said before, provided at that time. We only learned about the existence of this notebook in 2007. I just wanted to make that clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President and thank you Mr. Thayer. We'll come to his statement later and we'll look at all the documents the witness attached when he was giving the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you know of the existence of a demilitarisation agreement between the Army of Republika Srpska and the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Federation concerning Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've just answered that, I don't know. But if it's in a different way, I don't know, but I've already answered that. If you want me to repeat it, I'll do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go on, repeat it. I'm asking you, are you aware. There's nothing to repeat. Are you aware?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether I know of an existence of a demilitarisation agreement and I said that the demilitarisation that I knew of was what was in the cease-fire agreement. I did not get to see any other document on demilitarisation that is between the Bosnian Serb army and the Muslim side. I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show in e-court D21 so that the witness can finally see this agreement in accordance with which he was supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this will be coming up, Mr. Tolimir, you have used 1D286 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D216"], are you tendering that document, it's the Security Council resolution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we are tendering it because it was contested both by the Prosecution and the witness that it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, we want to hear the D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 2 in e-court, please. Only in Serbian, the English page remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see in Serbian this document which says: "Agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa concluded between lieutenant -- sorry, Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic in the presence of Philippe Morillon." It's a demilitarisation agreement. Let us look at the preamble. "Confirming their will to establish peace within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as stated in the agreement between contracting parties concluded on May 8, 1993. "Confirming Resolution 824 of the Security Council in which its declared that the towns of Zepa and Srebrenica and their surroundings should be treated as safe areas by all the parties concerned and should be free from armed attacks and from any other hostile act. "Confirming also that the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and the protocol additional to the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and relating to the protection of victims of international armed conflicts, (Protocol I), are fully applicable in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina." From the preamble of this agreement signed by General Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic. Would you please tell us, was this agreement based on the decisions included in the UN Security Council resolution on the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you can already see the section that you read concerning confirming Resolution 824 of the Security Council in which is declared that the towns of Zepa and Srebrenica and their surroundings would be treated as safe areas by all the parties concerned. So this was through a UN resolution which we already had, and also the cease-fire agreement, as I've already said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it clear from this agreement that the signatories wish the balance of power between Muslim and Serb forces be in conformity with Geneva Conventions and its additional protocol?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my understanding that is not what it means. If you look at the way it's worded, if it was to ensure parity, then we could not have declared one side a safe area. The UN would not have declared one side the safe area, it's got to be the same. That's both inside the enclave and outside. But now you can see one side has been declared a safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you whether the signatories wanted to base this agreement on Geneva Conventions and Protocol number 1 as written in the preamble as their commitment. Now, what the Security Council decided, whether they will have parity or not, I cannot go into that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly request you reframe the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will. Why did the signatories choose Protocol number 1 rather than Protocol number 2, because the Geneva Conventions have both? They chose Protocol number 1, do you know why? If you don't know, it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know why they chose one resolution. I don't know the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Protocol 1 stipulates demilitarisation, whereas Protocol number 2 does not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that Article 60 of that Protocol number 1, indicated here, of the Geneva Conventions governs the issue of establishment of demilitarised zones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue at hand is somehow different from the -- I mean, how we are -- where we are heading, in that the demilitarisation had already been done. Whether it was through whichever protocol or whichever resolution, demilitarisation had already been done even by the time we arrived there. It was done and it can be seen even in the documentation that is already with us. It had already been done. So it really does not matter whether a certain protocol or a certain resolution allowed or did not allow demilitarisation. The fact is it had already been done. And we were there to observe whether there would be any violations to the cease-fire agreement and report about it. And we carried out our tasks as far as our mandate allowed us. So we were not in any violation to any protocol or resolution. We just did our work according to what our mandate told us to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think Colonel Kingori has been very clear that he understood that they were operating under a cease-fire agreement which made somehow reference to a demilitarisation agreement. He has made clear that was all encompassing. He is now being shown a demilitarisation agreement which he may not have seen before, we don't know because General Tolimir hasn't asked him whether he has ever seen this before, in fact. He has been asked now questions about Protocol 1 and Protocol 2 of the Geneva Conventions. Colonel Kingori has answered to the best of his knowledge. I think if we keep on this line of questioning about subparts of the protocols in an agreement that we don't even know whether Colonel Kingori has seen, is not going to be productive. If there's some specific point that General Tolimir is trying to make or if there's some understanding he is trying to arrive at, then maybe there's a better question that can be asked. But asking him academic questions about whether a subpart of Protocol 1 incorporates something I'm not sure is particularly helpful, particularly when we haven't established whether this witness has seen this agreement before -- this specific agreement before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you've heard the concern of Mr. Thayer. You should try to use your time for cross-examination in the best way to get answers from this witness what he can tell you what you want to know. That's all what I want to say. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My legal assistant will find exactly the reference where I asked the witness, and I asked him explicitly, have you ever seen the demilitarisation agreement, and then I showed it to him saying, here you can see it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have all that on the record. Please continue your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but in his objection Mr. Thayer said I never asked the witness if he had seen it. I want to say for the record that I did. And second, I have the right to test the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, you have the right. This is not in dispute. Please carry on questioning the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please look at section 1 where it says: "The Demilitarised Zone." In English, you can see the heading halfway through the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Did the witness see this, and now I can ask a specific question. Does this designate specifically what the demilitarised areas are and does it say indeed demilitarise the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, if you look at what is written there, it indicates the areas of the -- the demilitarised areas of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of this objection that was voiced on page 23, I asked the witness about this agreement that we are now looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us based on what you've just read and seen here whether, when taking up your duties of UNMO in Srebrenica, did you know the exact borders of the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica and were they marked as such on the ground and on the map that you used?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown. We went round all the whole of the enclave and we also went through all the -- the whole cease-fire line and all the observation posts that had been put by the DutchBat so at least we could be able to know where, and on the map it was indicated very clearly, but on ground we saw it also.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show Article 3. We are not going to read all of this agreement, but Article 3 of this agreement signed by General Mladic and General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here is Article 3. It says: "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit/hand over their weapons. Ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR." Is it clear that all lethal weapons should be turned over to UNPROFOR in the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I've said that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Below there is a passage: "The hand-over of all weapons shall be observed by a team of three officers from both sides together with UNPROFOR officers." Does that mean that UNPROFOR was supposed to take and collect all the weapons and ammunition as written in Article 3?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that. All it says is that submitting or handing over of weapons will be observed, not carried out by, but observed, by a team of three officers from both sides together with UNPROFOR officers who will arrange the places where the hand-over will be done. So the UNPROFOR is to arrange where the weapons would be put, and in this case, what I know is that it was done by and put in the B Company compound of the DutchBat. So UNPROFOR did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the -- in fact, if the UNPROFOR did not do that, was the Army of Republika Srpska supposed to go into the zone and take away all the weapons as written in Article 1?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me it's a bit difficult to understand that question. I don't know whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. Since the agreement expresses a mutual wish of both sides, did the other side, in this case the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially communicate to UNPROFOR or the observers that they had turned over all the weapons, ammunition, and combat supplies from the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's good, Your Honour, to get the whole thing from the beginning, in that there was a series of military observers and even the battalions being changed from time to time. So you can see this was done in 1993. 1993 I was not anywhere close to that place. So the process that was followed should have been, according to my understanding, in accordance with what is written here. We, as military observers who went there, and I personally went there in 1995, so me, I found an already demilitarised place with the weapons in one area. So to say whether it was followed or whatever, I cannot be able to tell. All I know is that ... if I can continue. All I know is that demilitarisation had already been done and all the weapons were put in one particular area, as had also been done in other areas in former Yugoslavia. So that, to the best of my knowledge, it had been done. Furthermore, the handing over of these weapons to this particular place -- you know, because the way you asked the question is like the Bosnian Serb army had to go inside there. Really, how they had done it, I do not know. But demilitarisation had already been done. We witnessed that it had been done. The weapons were put in one particular place, and there was a list of all those weapons which were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that that was the case in all demilitarised zones in the former Yugoslavia. Did units surrender in Tuzla, which was also a protected area, in the same way as they did in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My belief is that it was the same in all the UN protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know or did you just believe that the same things happened in Bihac, Tuzla, Sarajevo? Did you know it for a fact or is this just your opinion, something that you think happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I believe, and in case you are seeking my opinion, I did not observe it. I did not go there in those other areas, so if you want me to be specific, I just know about Srebrenica. I can talk about Sector East, that is the Eastern Slavonia, because at least those areas I worked there. But what I said is that I believe. I do not know. I never observed in those other areas that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I know the Prosecution is really a broken record on this issue, Mr. President, but I just want to note again for the record that the fact that the Srebrenica enclave was not fully demilitarised is not a matter in contest as far as the Prosecution is concerned. This Chamber has ruled in its 17 December 2009 decision on adjudicated facts, and I would note numbers 46, 47 and 48, that the demilitarisation was conducted but not all weapons were turned in, that there were helicopters regularly flying, that the 28th Division was rearming itself and so forth. Again, General Tolimir is free to choose how to use his time, but we have spent I don't know how long on this issue of demilitarisation and it is, frankly, again, not in dispute as far as the Prosecution is concerned. And Colonel Kingori has exhaustively detailed his understanding of that process and what he observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much that you are drawing all our attention to the decision on adjudicated facts, but now I think it's an appropriate time to have the first break and I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir to take into account what just -- what Mr. Thayer was just mentioning. We adjourn and resume at 11.00. Someone will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Sorry, there must be one correction made for the sake of the record by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The last Defence exhibit admitted, D114, is 65 ter 1D286 and not 1D216 as recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Madam Registrar, and now could I reply to the Prosecutor's remark in only 30 seconds or less. In the testimony of this witness, the witness has spoken on several occasions about the parity of forces and the need for the parity. And he has also said that the demilitarisation was over, that all the arms landed with Bravo Company and it's all on the record. I had to test the credibility of the witness who was a military observer who was supposed to observe the situation. He still claims and he keeps on claiming things that simply are not the fact, and even the Prosecutor admits that they are not, and that's why I had to test the credibility of the witness because I wanted to point to some things and possibly to see whether there is a bias when he is speaking about a parity because he is supposed to be dealing and talking about a military agreement which was accepted by all the sides. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether, Your Honour, you can allow me to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should wait for the next question by Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us, Zepa and Srebrenica -- or, rather, only Srebrenica was a protected area, and in addition to that, did the sides also agree for Srebrenica to be a demilitarised zone by means of that agreement, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all is that I may require to start with clarifying on something that you've said, that I talked about need for parity between the forces of the Bosnian Serbs and the Muslim side. I did not say that and I have not said that during the course of my stay here. I've not said that, that there was need for parity. Secondly, on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, please note that it was demilitarised. It was a UN protected area. Whether it was fully demilitarised, as I said yesterday, is what one cannot be able to understand because at least we could see some people with small arms and it's also in our situation reports that we could see them. So mopping up every bit of weapon, every bit of fire-arm, it's a bit difficult in normal circumstances, but at least most of the weapons were handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And my next question based on your previous answer is this: When you saw the small weapons, as you have described it, in the hands of militarily able men, did you report about that to anybody, and did you seize it from them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As military observers, we did what we were supposed to do; that is, report about those weapons, not seize them. Our work was not to seize the weapons, but we reported and is on record, is in some of my sitreps -- in our sitreps and also in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question based on your previous answer is this: Did there come a time for you to make it known to the Army of Republika Srpska, as one of the parties to the agreement, that Muslims were openly carrying weapons in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact I've not even said they were openly carrying weapons. It was just a few instances that we noted that they were carrying some weapons. It's not always. So in that time we reported to our headquarters about it and for the -- on the side of the Bosnian Serb army, we never discussed that, but if there was need for that, we still could have discussed it because in most cases when you meet the other side, regardless of whether it's the Bosnian Serbs or the Muslims, there are some issues you really do not have to discuss with them. But provided we have reported to the UN headquarters, we had done our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce Article 5 of this agreement, paragraph 4 and 5 of the demilitarisation agreement. We can now see paragraph 5. Can the court please produce the following page in the Serbian language. Thank you. The following page in the Serbian language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are looking at the first paragraph on this page: "Non-combatants except members of UNPROFOR who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone are not permitted to have in their possession any weapons, ammunition or explosives. Weapons, ammunition and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR. Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone." Thank you. Based on what we've just seen, this provision of the agreement that was signed by both sides, we can see that there was a ban. And did that ban apply to all combatants, and that non-combatants who are found with weapons, explosives or other lethal weapons should have those seized from them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was to be done, but I may require to remind you again that I was a military observer, not UNPROFOR. So our work was not to seize any weapons. Ours was to report and we used to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, this is exactly what I'm asking from you, to say exactly how things were. My next question is this: Was Ramiz Becirovic a combatant?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what you mean by a combatant. In the sense that him being a Chief of Staff of the Muslim Army, really he belonged to the Bosnian Muslims army. So I don't get you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Please look at the paragraph in English where it says: "Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone." That's the last -- did you find it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Last sentence of Article 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope you are talking about where it's written, and I may read: "Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone, except members of UNPROFOR, are not permitted to have in their possession any weapons, ammunition or explosives. Weapons, ammunition and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR." If that's where you are referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, to the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Combatants will not be allowed to enter or be in the demilitarised zones." And that's why I said Chief of Staff, that is, Ramiz, belonged to the army. But you become a -- and that's why I asked you what you mean by a combatant because if you are not in the war position, in the war posture, if you are not armed, you are not, as far as I can understand, a combatant. You can be a rival to the other group but you are not a combatant because you are not fighting. You are not ready to fight. So as far as we were concerned, Ramiz was not armed whenever we met. He was never in uniform, so he was not a combatant. But he belonged to an army, but he was not a combatant. He was not in a ready-to-fight position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the definition of a combatant in terms of the international law? If you don't, it doesn't matter. I'm asking you just whether you do know or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning of the word "combatant" varies, and the way I understand it in this situation is that it's someone who is ready for war, someone who is ready for combat, because combatant is -- you know, combat is war. And you cannot be ready for war if you are not, first of all, in uniform, you are not armed, and you don't have an army. You don't have a combatant force with you, so you cannot be a combatant at that particular moment. That does not necessarily mean that later on when you go and get into uniform, arm yourself, and lead an army, that you were not a combatant. But at that particular moment, earlier, as I've said, you are not a combatant at all. As far as I understand the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. This is the first time I hear that Becirovic was not a combatant, although he was a Chief of Staff. However, in your opinion, is a combatant a person who bears arms but does not wear a uniform? In other words, can you be a combatant if you fight in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will still try to answer that question and say what I said earlier. You know, if you are not in uniform, you are not in a ready-to-fight posture. You are not in a combat mode. You really cannot be termed a "combatant." You and myself, yeah, we are not combatants. But you have a military history, I have a military history, but we are not combatants because we are not in a ready-to-fight condition or situation. So not everybody you see around is a combatant just because he has military experience or he has a position in the military, no. That is my understanding. And even if you go out there and find Dutch soldiers, even outside here, who are not in uniform and they're not ready for combat and there's no war that particular day, they are not fighting, really you can't call that person a combatant, as far as I can understand the situation and as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's talk about a very specific situation. Did you ever see a person, a civilian in Srebrenica bearing arms? And was that person in a ready-to-fight position? What makes a person in a ready-to-fight position in your view? Does it mean that he is bearing arms or that he is wearing a uniform? What is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think the witness has explained his position, his understanding of the word "combatant," and therefore I think it's really a pure repetition if you put this question to the witness again. He explained it extensively. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witnesses, fighters from Srebrenica have been here and spoke about bearing arms in civilian clothes because their town was a demilitarised zone, and I can appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, a military observer -- should military observers be familiar with the Geneva Conventions, and were you familiar with the provisions of Protocol 1, paragraph 60, Article 7 of that protocol? I'm going to read it to you just in case because one cannot always remember things. I will read it. I'm reading from Article 60, paragraph 7 of the additional Protocol 1. This is an additional protocol to the Geneva Conventions, and I quote: "If one warring party makes -- violates provisions 3 or 6, the other side will be exempted from their obligations pursuant to the agreement." For the sake of the interpreters I repeat. Article 6, paragraph 7 of the Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions. "If a warring party violates the provisions 3 or 6, the other side will be exempted from their commitments stemming from the agreement assigning to a zone the status of a protected area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we are going to have a class quiz on the Geneva Conventions and the protocols, I think it's only fair to the witness not to read sections that in turn refer to other sections that aren't being put to the witness. If General Tolimir is truly interested in finding out what this witness has to say or think about certain provisions, then he should do him the courtesy of showing him what he is talking about. He just read a section that refers to provisions 3 or 6. We don't have the articles handy, they weren't on the list. It is extremely unhelpful to the witness to proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in addition, the Chamber is in the same position, we don't know what is the full text. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Geneva Conventions have not been uploaded in e-court because this is an international law that is applied by this Tribunal. It would be crazy to ask for its admission into evidence, and Mr. Tolimir is simply testing the witness's credibility by checking his knowledge of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand the position of the Defence but there should be a more appropriate way to deal with that and it is the right of the Defence to challenge the credibility. That is the main purpose of the whole cross-examination, of course. But reading a certain part of a document into the record, it is not helpful to -- if you want to challenge the credibility of the witness. You should do it in another way and just put questions about his knowledge. Ask him if he knows anything about that, then you will get an answer. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Mr. President, the Prosecution has no problems, obviously, with the accused testing the credibility of any witness. That's not what is at issue here. What is at issue is the manner in which General Tolimir is going about it. This is not a game of gotcha, and if he has got a copy of the protocols in hard copy that he is reading from, then maybe we can just put it on the ELMO; or if there are particular sections that he can read in full, although that's going to be cumbersome because we've got three now that are referred to, then he should put that on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you provide the witness with the text?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the text before me. If necessary, I will upload the document tomorrow in e-court with the help of my assistants. I can go on reading. I have read from the original text of the protocol which is an integral part of the agreement, and I quoted from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tolimir, if you want to have a clear answer from this witness, you should give him the chance to read that specific part of the Geneva Convention. If you have a hard copy, give it with the assistance of the Usher to the witness, put it on the ELMO, and we can proceed. Otherwise, it's not very helpful just to quote from a quite unknown text. We don't have the full text in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for having allowed the witness to see the document. I had to clarify the matter because I'm interested in the rights of the parties at the time when the witness discharged his mission of a military observer. I was simply interested in the rights of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, this is not in dispute, Mr. Tolimir, but everybody wants to know what you are reading from. And therefore we see it now on the ELMO. The Defence has given the text to the Court Usher and I hope we can follow what you are now referring to. It is not on the ELMO yet. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the text is in the Serbian language. I'll try and find it in the English as well within the next couple of minutes and forward it to the Registry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think if you have it only in the Serbian language it will be a problem for the witness to read it, and if then -- the other way around, please. Yes. Thank you. But the witness can't read it. Mr. Gajic has indicated that he will try to get an English translation, the English version of that. Perhaps we wait -- you should wait with these questions until you have an English version. Perhaps you deal in the meantime with another topic. It's not helpful to have this on the ELMO. We can remove it. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. While Mr. Gajic is looking for the text in English, can I ask for an MFI. P82 [as interpreted]. We don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, there might be a problem on the record. It is recorded "P82," but I suppose you are referring to D82; is that correct? Because D82 is on your exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be on the screen. Now we have it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We see it in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see that this document is dated 29 April 1995. It was sent to the 2nd Corps command to Brigadier Sead Delic personally. And when we look at the signature, we will see that it was written by Salihovic. Salihovic. My question is: Did you have occasion to meet Mr. Ekrem Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that he signed this document. My second question is, on this date indicated here, 29 April 1995, were you a UN military observer in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I was there. I arrived in April and I think I was there at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the first sentence, please. It says: "In your letter, the number and date stated above, we received orders for action regarding discontinuation of engineering works on the UN observation post in the Lozina village sector, on the Srebrenica-Zepa DMZ corridor." Do you know anything about this corridor and about the building of an engineered UN observation post near Lozina village?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be unable to remember the Lozina village, as such, but, you know, building a UN observation post, that was a continuous thing. In areas where we required our observation post to see what was happening on the other side, we would request that, you know, not us as military observers, but UNPROFOR would request for that. At times when some of these posts were not serving the observers well, we would request another area to be worked on. But on this particular area called Lozina, unless maybe I look at the map, I may be unable to remember this particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know anything about a corridor which is mentioned in this first paragraph and which was part of the question of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Srebrenica-Zepa demilitarised zone corridor. The only thing I can remember about such a corridor is that there was a route that was being used by some of the Muslims to get out to Zepa to get supplies into the enclave. This was being done in collaboration with the Bosnian Serbs army. That is, they could be paid something and they allow the Muslims to go out to that corridor to Zepa. I think this is the corridor which is being referred to. And also on their safe reentry into the enclave with the supplies. At times when these payments were not made well or maybe were not honoured, the Muslims would be attacked on their way back and that is the time we would be called that the Muslims have been attacked in such and such a place. But when we investigate further we find that it was because of that non-payment. So there was a corridor. There was somewhere that they were passing through to Zepa and back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir. One moment, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Can you just elaborate a little bit on payments were made, what kind of payment, from whom to whom? And if you know, for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
