utterances.text: Your Honour, these were illegal payments which were being made. Like it was -- we used to call it like mafia type, in that there should actually be no exit or entry from that enclave, but because of a lack of supplies, and sometimes even the UNHCR convoys were not allowed into the enclave, these people had to devise ways of going out. These merchants had to devise ways of going out. And it's almost everywhere, in any war situation you find that some people who organise ways of getting out to get supplies from outside, come and sell in the enclave, because the people in the enclave do not have those supplies. So it was like a mafia in quotes, an organisation, an arrangement that, We will give you safe passage to Zepa, but you pay this amount. So they used to do that, and we knew it and we used to report about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We'll come later to the humanitarian problems. I'm asking you now if you know anything about the building of the UNPROFOR observation post in the area we've just read about when the Muslims forbade them to continue building?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue raised was on the actual occasion, that is the Lozina village, but if this is another location that I can still remember where there was a tug of war between the Muslims and the UNPROFOR, this was a section whereby the UNPROFOR, that is the DutchBat, wanted to build another observation post, but inside, slightly more inside from the cease-fire line inside the enclave. And the Muslims were not happy about that because they were saying this will draw the Serb -- the BSA more towards -- more inside the enclave. So if this is the one that I'm remembering, there was such a post and the Muslims were not happy about it. They were asking the UN -- the UNPROFOR to build it where it was before or slightly further into the cease-fire line, but not inside the enclave. Now, for the UNPROFOR, the reason why they wanted to build it slightly farther inside is because of the incursions by the Bosnian Serbs army. So they felt more unsafe more towards the cease-fire line than towards the Srebrenica area of responsibility. So it was -- I think that was the main problem that was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You presented two options here. In the first option the Muslims wanted to keep these, as you call them, mafia channels open. And in the second option they did not want the observation post to be built because they were afraid of the Bosnian Serb army. Now, which of these two applies to the issue of the building of the UN observation post in the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that is how you got it, that is not the way I said it. On the mafia channels, I said about the arrangements, the private arrangements which were there between the Muslims and the Bosnian Serb army. On the observation post, I did not say the Muslims did not want that post to be erected there so that they may not be observed, but they wanted it moved to where it was before; that is, more inside the cease-fire line but not inside the enclave. Your Honour, if I may describe that a bit. There was the side of the Muslims and on the opposite side, obviously, the side of the Serbs. But in between there was a corridor that we used to call the cease-fire line. That cease-fire line went around the whole enclave and we used to mark it. We had marked it with grid references and we knew where they were. So the observation posts were supposed to be in the cease-fire line. It was not just as one line, it was a corridor, sort of. But now the DutchBat were getting shelled from the BSA side and they felt it safer to move slightly inside the enclave. But to the Muslims it was like they were ceding ground for the BSA and that ground was to be protected by the DutchBat. So they were telling DutchBat, You cannot move more inside the enclave, we cannot allow you to come and build this observation post here. Maybe that is the explanation maybe I needed to explain. But if there was something that I have not answered from your question, please ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you again, did the Muslims protest the engineering of the UN observation post because of the mafia channels, from the question of Judge Nyambe, or because they were afraid that the Bosnian Serb army would penetrate into the depth of the protected area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's because they felt the Bosnian Serb army would move more inside. They would be drawn more towards the enclave than they were before. That is, they had their own positions, dug in positions, you know, areas where they had their trenches, and now if the DutchBat moved slightly inside, they would be pulled slightly more inside into the cease-fire line and maybe into the Muslim side of the enclave, that is, in their protected area, and that was the fear. It was not because of the observation of the mafia type. I don't know but if it was, then I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This document speaks for itself. It indicates clearly whether the reason was what you say or something else. Let's look a paragraph 5 of this document: "Our side insisted that the UN representatives should unconditionally discontinue further engineering works on the observation post in question and withdraw all personnel from the location until a suitable solution is found." They are not talking, therefore, about moving it forward or backward but they want the UN personnel to withdraw completely from there, from the separation line. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe you can give me a few minutes to go through this document, if you might.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There will be questions about other passages, but I'm repeating this one. "Our side insisted that the UN representatives" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, please don't repeat. It is on the record and the witness can see it on the screen. Don't waste time by repeating.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you please read the sentence that I quoted and then tell us, was the UNPROFOR asked here to move forward or backward or was it asked to withdraw completely?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This observation post, if it is the one I'm remembering, is the one I talked about earlier. And I thought maybe you could assist me by maybe placing a map so that I can -- we can be able to locate the place, but if it was not, then the aim was actually to establish an observation post. The way I still remember it is in that light, that is, it was to be moved more inside and that is where they are just talking about the construction of the OP. But there were so many OPs in the area, and you have a list of all of them. So which one are you referring to, if I may ask, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I said I meant the one they were building in Lozina village. I can show you on the map where it was. You said there was a corridor between Zepa and Srebrenica there, that's why I didn't show you the map. But this speaks about unconditional withdrawal of the UNPROFOR and unconditional termination of the building. Unconditional withdrawal. It goes on to say: "Our proposal was fully supported by the chief of military observers, Romilton of Brazil, while the UN liaison officer partially accepted the proposal. That is, he agreed to discontinue further construction of the observation post, as long as he was able to keep his personnel there and use the location as such for observation until an adequate solution was found." If this reminds you of anything, do you know who this Mr. Romilton from Brazil is who was the chief of UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do. I do remember Romilton. He was our team leader. And as is quoted here, he went for that meeting, but I don't know any other reason other than one I've given. But I could have done better if you showed me the map or put the -- the OP and its number, OP Alpha, Romeo, whatever, as is given in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's the third time that this witness has asked for a very simple thing to assist him in answering these repeated questions from General Tolimir. General Tolimir instead has continued his line of questioning on this passage. I would simply ask General Tolimir to comply with a very simple question and request from this witness. General Tolimir clearly has an exact idea and knowledge of where this location is, what OP it's next to and what area of the enclave it's in. It's not a game of gotcha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you in a position to help the witness with a map or leave this topic because you have got the answer I think two or three times to your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will certainly show him the map. I was just asking, while we are waiting for that map, if he knew who Romilton was and whether he had had any role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You got the answer. It's no -- no, it is not necessary to repeat anything. You've got an answer to all your questions. I think you have many more questions to put. You should continue with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My assistant will give us a reference to that map that was drawn here by UNPROFOR deputy commander and which has been exhibited. While my legal assistant is looking for this exhibit, could we show P83 -- D83, sorry. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you leave this document on the screen, that was also marked for identification because the previous witness Nicolai couldn't say anything about the content. Are you tendering that now as an exhibit, which is still on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document D82, marked for identification, will become an exhibit in this case. Now, we move to D83.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without abandoning the subject, can we show P65 first, and that's the map that the witness wanted to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should check the number again. It is not a map with this number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D. D. D65. Thank you. Would it be possible to zoom in on this triangle and these arrows and the markings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see now the observation post that was placed -- do you remember if there was a corridor on this side between Zepa and Srebrenica, if you look at the map and the separation line?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I can remember the corridor. It was more towards my right near the bottom. That is where the corridor was towards Zepa. The names there, I cannot be able to read them properly but where it's written "1 Papa Bravo," something like that, that is where the corridor was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you draw in green, if you have that colour, where you think the corridor was in a dotted line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can it please be enlarged in the area between the south-west part of the enclave before it will be marked. The left part of the map. To enable the witness to read the names. The left bottom part of the left bottom quarter of this. I think it's better. And now move it a little bit up and to the left. Yes, a little bit further. Thank you. I think that should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was the general area, and this, from this other side. This was the corridor, as far as I can, you know, try to remember it now towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very sorry, that was perhaps my mistake that I focussed on the left side. It should be the right side. We should do it again and so that we have a full picture. Can that be moved, the map, to the left side so that we see more of the right side of the map. No, the other way around. Further, further, further, further, further. Further. Sir, is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is sufficient. And I hope the directions -- because I cannot read the names, the direction, I think, is still maybe a bit of an orientation. The north should be the way it is on the map, that is from bottom to top, I think. And if it is, then the corridor remains the way I had marked earlier, that is, this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now try it again, please. Something wrong with the pen. Or with the system. It's lost again. I think that's fine. And now wait a moment so that the Court Usher can assist you to prepare the system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the general corridor towards Zepa the way I can remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the corridor please be drawn in a dotted line for everybody to see. I can't see that the witness has drawn anything. Thank you. The corridor has to cross the separation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness has drawn two lines. Perhaps to make it clear, I would like to ask the witness to put a number 1 to one line and to put a number 2 to the other line so that we have a clear indication and can compare it with the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But here, Your Honour, is not a matter of -- the two lines are actually indicating -- what is important is what is in the middle because that was the corridor. It was a wide corridor because they were not using one route. But it was a wide corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this map be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked map will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D115.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please draw the observation post, where was it? The one for which the Muslims asked for the interruption of engineering works, and can you mark it with a letter Z.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot be able to remember all the observation posts in this area, but if we go to the grid references, I can easily be able to mark it. But right now, I cannot be able to remember the actual location of the OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tomorrow we'll prepare the exact co-ordinates of the location that other witnesses have spoken about and that the document we have in front of us also speaks about and then you will be able to do it, because if we were to do it now, it would take a lot of time for my assistants to do. And before that, while we are looking at the map, maybe you can answer me this: What was the military significance of this corridor, and why did the commanders have to write to their superior command to secure it? Was that corridor used only for smuggling or was it also used for other purposes as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are similar questions like you had asked earlier but I will still answer it, that we knew this corridor was used for smuggling of goods or bringing in goods from outside the enclave, mainly from Zepa to the enclave. So this was the main -- the main activity that was going on here. As I said, the corridor was wide, it was not a line. It was wide because they could not use the same road all the time, they had to change, use the forest, the cover of the forest and all that so that they felt secure, but it was wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for putting two questions to you in one. My question was this: Did that corridor have any military significance since Muslims requested from their command to put a stop to the engineering reinforcement of the UN observation post in that corridor? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness made very clear during several answers that there were two distinct issues. One was the creation of a new observation post instead of the one in the demilitarised zone. And the other was the corridor for smuggling. The witness stated there was no relation between the two issues. Please go ahead with your questions. If you have received an answer, even if it's not satisfactory for your purposes, that might happen in the course of such a trial, but please focus on something different now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm asking, I've not received an answer and the question is this: Did the corridor between Srebrenica and Zepa have any military significance? Thank you. I've not received an answer to this question, Your Honour. I don't really mind what answer I may receive, but I've not received an answer to the question about the military significance of the corridor, and the witness perhaps knows the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are right. You didn't receive an answer to this specific part of your question. The problem is that you did connect this question with an explanation of your understanding of the whole situation and that creates some confusion. This question was not answered and we would like to hear an answer if there is a specific -- if there is significance in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the military part that he is talking about is a bit unclear, whether it's from the Muslim side or from the Bosnian Serb army, but in military terms, I can say any road, any high ground is a ground of tactical importance. We call it, and he knows it, a GTI, a ground of tactical importance, in that you can use it for any military activity. And so for the Bosnian Serb army it could have been a very important road. For the Muslims it could have been a very important road, because roads are very important for in the military. So I don't know which military he is talking about, but generally, for military purposes, a road is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My I ask you in this way: Was this corridor used by the Muslim Army for transporting military devices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that is the question, we were not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, could you please say whether this observation point had any military significance for UNPROFOR? Were they able to observe military activities from that observation post that they were in the process of building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Until, Mr. President, the witness is able to locate what this OP is to which General Tolimir is referring, any answer he gives is going to be very limited in its helpfulness to the Trial Chamber. This document that General Tolimir has been working with refers to a village of Lozina. That's the location we're talking about. I don't remember off the top of my head where that's located. The map that General Tolimir has shown the witness is so blurred that the witness cannot identify the OPs themselves. I'm given to understand that there will be a more legible map maybe tomorrow, but until the witness has any idea about what OP General Tolimir is talking about, it's not going to be helpful to this Trial Chamber. And if General Tolimir knows where this location, and I'm sure he does, why doesn't he just tell the witness or point it out on the record for the witness, so that we can move on and have some productive answers for the Trial Chamber as opposed to keeping everybody guessing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would that be a helpful suggestion by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not want to suggest anything to the witness. I am merely testing his credibility. I would like to tell him [as interpreted] whether he remembers any problems with the removal of the UNPROFOR OP and the construction of another one which was better constructed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have heard many answers. Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Thayer asked you for something else. You have heard everything what the witness can tell you about this observation post and creation of a new one. Can you indicate where this village of Lozina is on the map? Then you could perhaps get an answer to that question, the link to the corridor and the smuggling of weapons. But without indicating where it could be, it is, I think, impossible for the witness. He told you he doesn't know where it is because he doesn't remember the name Lozina. Help the witness and don't repeat what you have said many times.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If the witness says that he doesn't remember a dispute with regard to the construction of an OP within the demilitarised zone, I'm happy with that. I will not ask for a better answer. I'm just very nicely asking the witness, I showed him the map that another witness marked as a location in dispute and as an observation post in dispute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have stopped you because this is again a misrepresentation. The witness didn't deny anything about a dispute on the question of this observation post. There was a problem and he testified about that. We are dealing with an absolutely different matter, where is the village Lozina. Help the witness to identify it because he doesn't remember the location of this village and then you will perhaps get an additional answer. But you have heard everything in this respect already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, whatever I show the witness in the map he will not be able to follow me. I have to get a different map. That's why I said that my assistant would try to make sure to find a better map. You can see how illegible this map is, and I've shown the witness a sector that was drawn by a witness before him and he also marked that sector. There's nothing else that I can show him. I can only try to jog his memory by additional questions that might help him remember the location. Until I'm able to find a new map, there's nothing I can do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then please carry on with the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will move on and tomorrow we will come back to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, as a military observer of the United Nations, did you know whether people were sent to the demilitarised zones to carry out sabotage operations in the rear of the Army of Republika Srpska, or actually, whether people from the demilitarised zones were dispatched on sabotage missions behind the enemy lines, behind the lines of the Army of Republika Srpska outside of the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember receiving such reports, but it's possible they used to carry them out. You cannot dismiss such an issue. That is, if your enemy is encroaching more on your side, there's a possibility that you try to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know -- and I did not say that either us or somebody else sent you a document to that effect. We are not authorised to do that. But I'm asking you whether you know of any military activities originating from the demilitarised zones and directed against the Army of Republika Srpska; if yes, did you report about that to your superiors? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope my memory is serving me right, and I don't remember reports coming in from the Bosnian Serb side on an issue with activities coming from inside the enclave towards the Bosnian Serb army. I don't remember receiving any report of attacks from the Muslim side on the Bosnian Serb army. Unlike what we used to receive from the Muslims of perpetration of force against them by the Bosnian Serb army, attacks coming from the Bosnian Serb army towards the enclave. That is in our reports. But on the other way around, I don't remember any complaint coming to us from the BSA side. On activities to do with the military, that is the Bosnian Serb army, is well documented and in various reports that we made we could hear shells coming in. We could get reports of people injured in the enclave by incoming shells from the BSA positions. That we used to get and we used to report about it. But the other way around, really, I don't remember. And if there was, it was minimal. I'm not very sure, but I don't think there was very much activity coming from inside the enclave towards the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the Army of Republika Srpska, was it supposed to be in communication with you personally, with UNPROFOR, or with somebody else who was in charge of communications across the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had direct connection with BSA through an interpreter called Petar who had radio communication. He could contact us any time there's need. Any time there is a requirement for a meeting with either Major Nikolic or whenever there's an issue that they wanted us as military observers to know, he could call us, and we could also at times call him to confirm a few issues. So we were in direct communication with BSA all the time, but as I said, through Mr. Petar, the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that direct communication between yourself and the brigade leaning on Srebrenica or between you and the Main Staff? In other words, were you in direct communication only in the -- with the Bratunac Brigade, but also with the Milici Brigade, the Vlasenica Brigade, the Rogatica Brigade, and all the others?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you are talking about communication with the other brigades, there has got to be an entry point and the entry point was only one, through the interpreter, that is Mr. Petar, who would communicate with Major Nikolic who was acting like the liaison officer. He was this charge of the battalion which was around there, as far as we knew, and he was the liaison between the military, the Bosnian Serb army, and UN military observers. So we had communication with him. But if you talk about the other military units of the Bosnian Serb who could have been around there or in the vicinity, we did not have any other communication other than through Major Nikolic who you could get, or he could get us, through Mr. Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the representatives of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, Tuzla or at any other level aware of the existence of that interpreter Mr. Petar, or was it just you and the UNMOs in Srebrenica who knew of his existence?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be difficult to know what you are driving at, but Petar was being paid by the UN, so if he was being paid, given allowances by the UN, obviously he was in the system. He was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If Petar was paid by the UN, then let me ask you this: Did the UN command in Srebrenica inform you about the complaints from Sarajevo about sabotage operations coming from inside Srebrenica towards the Serbian zone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there were complaints from the Sarajevo side, the UN military observers therein were to communicate with their headquarters, not with us. So if there was anything they observed, they were to send through the normal channels, not to us but to their headquarters. So maybe it can be checked with the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any feedback on any of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there was to be any feedback because there's nothing we had told them. I mean, according to my answer, it is the team which is on that other side to report about what was happening in that -- in their area of responsibility. They didn't have to send it to us. So what feedback maybe could you be talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. UNMO teams and UNMO individuals at any level, did you exchange information with the UNPROFOR about the activities in the zones that you were in charge of and where you carried out your observations and monitoring? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were not obliged to do anything like that. We could compare notes at unofficial levels, but really, a military team, a military observer team in a certain area, let's say in Sarajevo and one in Srebrenica, they didn't necessarily have to compare notes, but unofficially they could. Or one could see or access, if you wanted, a report by another team but not necessarily a must. It was not mandatory for you check what the other team is doing. But if I may add, if the headquarters got a report concerning a certain -- from a certain team and would want clarification from another team, they would send the same report and also maybe even add their own words to say, Please check on this, we have gotten a report about this, can you check on whether this is happening in your AOR. And then we would check it and confirm, or deny, or even say, We'll do further checks and then inform you. That could happen. But it's not necessarily that we had to communicate directly with the other teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we must have our second break. We will adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can the court please produce this witness's statement, P9992 [as interpreted], page 2, paragraph 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Once again, please, P999?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I said. I said 5992. Here it is on the screen. Page 2 in Serbian, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is Exhibit P992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You speak here about the number of refugees in Srebrenica and you say 42.000. Could you tell us, on what basis did you reach this number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we just need to advance a couple of more pages in the English to get to the right paragraph. It's page -- actually page number 2 of the document, so we need to go forward two pages more in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In Serbian, that's paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where it says: "You are showing me a document dated 8 July, summarising the situation on that date in terms of supplies. This document also contains general data about the number of people in the enclave. We got to the number of 42.000 by adding up the information received from the municipality. The numbers are broken down by villages and we also added the number of people who were accommodated in the Swedish Project. When we visited all these villages, we estimated that the figures given us were reliable. The structure of the local population, or rather, the ratio between the local population and refugees, 85 per cent, was given us by the municipality through Osman Suljic." I believe the witness remembers this now. And my question is, how did you arrive at the number 42.000? Would you please repeat for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a figure that we got after adding the information that we already had and what we got from the UNHCR and other UN agencies and NGOs which indicated the population village by village, the estimated population village by village and now we could summarise and get a total of around 42.000. So there was no census that was done but that is the way we came up with that figure, our working figure of 42.000 inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you say in your statement and now that you arrived at this figure through several sources, Osman Suljic, and the UNHCR, and your own visit to the villages, and the Swedish Project, and that all these figures are reliable in your estimate. That's what you say in that paragraph. My question is, did you at any time check the reliability of all these figures or did you just take their word for it that these figures are real?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only way that one could have tested the reliability of these figures was by doing a census which we could not do, which we did not do, but this was our working figure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D284 is the document we need next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And before it is displayed, did you at any time express doubts of the figures given you by the local authorities concerning the number of refugees, the number of civilians, the number of humanitarian workers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the case of doubting these figures, we know for sure, and even now it still continues, anywhere where humanitarian activities, you know, are going on, you can never be sure of the figures. You can never at any time say this is the exact figure. So we did not go out there to verify. But doubting, at times you can doubt some villages, maybe you can go at the Swedish Shelter and find maybe they look slightly fewer than normal. Maybe you go another village and maybe there are more. So unless you do a proper counting, this was to us a good working figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at some notes on this document. It says: "Please find attached the required information for statistical purposes which you should not submit for review to international organisations because we are calculating this number of 45.000." That's signed by the president of Srebrenica municipality Fahrudin Salihovic. Now, when you went on field missions, did you ask for lists or were you just told that the number is so and so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to -- since we have no translation in English, I would like to know what it is about, what we are looking at on the screen. You should indicate the heading and the date so that we know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is a letter from the Srebrenica municipality sent to the section for statistics in Tuzla, department for statistics, concerning figures for Srebrenica. And the first line says, Pursuant to your letter number such and such, we hereby provide the following data. 1, the number of local residents in the municipality, 9.791 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was not asking for that, but for the headline and you indicated that, and I see the date 11th of January, 1994. Thank you. And now the answer of the witness, please, if you recall it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just use what, Your Honour, what he has said because I cannot be able to understand what is in this language, but I would assume that what the interpretation has put is the correct one. You can see even the figure we have of around 42.000. The one they have of about 45.000 is very -- is pretty close. So with us, we got the figure when we arrived there. It was part of our brief because it had already been done and maybe reviewed until the time we arrived there when we got that figure. It was a brief that we got.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. We can see here that they showed to you a higher number of the population in order to get more humanitarian aid; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure you cannot discount that, you cannot discount that. So getting an additional figure of, I mean, 3.000 on top, it can make sense. Or maybe even the figure was the correct one, we are not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. They say that they are presenting to you 45.000, whereas in the text above they show how many people they have in fact. But let us look at 1D285 instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering this document we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will tender them together because this document explains how much population there was in fact. The document we've just seen says that they are presenting the number of 45.000, and this one speaks about the real figures. This document has not been translated, but it's from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, municipality of Srebrenica, and it was sent on the 11th of January, 1995, the municipal staff of civilian protection, Srebrenica. And it says: "Summary of the number of population and households by municipality local and displaced population, numbers of dead, registered at check-points, the number of dead soldiers and civilians (where some information is available on the place and manner of death and place of burial)."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, the first box in this table gives the total number of population and that's 36.051, considerably less than 45.000. This was signed by the municipal staff for civilian protection in Srebrenica. Tell me, what duty did Osman Suljic, who you mentioned in your testimony, occupy in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew him as the mayor of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question is, since in this document for which you have no translation, I read that they had a total of 36.051 residents. To you they said they had 42.000, and they also said they are presenting 45.000 to international organisations. The difference is almost 11.000. And between the number that you estimated and the actual figure the difference is about 6.000. How do you explain this difference between the actual number of residents, the number you gave in your statement, and the number they presented to international organisations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand when you say "the actual number," because unless you tell me now what the actual number was, is it 36.000, is that the figure you want to work on? Is that the figure you are taking as the actual figure? And if so, then you must be having a reason for doing that. Is it the 45.000? Is it the 42? Because it seems you already have a stand of the 36.051 as being the actual figure. We, from the UN side, when I was there, the figure we had was 42, so me, I remain with the 42. And the other figures, me, I don't know. I don't -- I'm not privy to what was written in these documents. I didn't see these documents, I don't know them. So me, I remain with the 42 that we estimated. And we got good reasons to have such estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not make any assertions on my own behalf, in my own name, because I don't have the right to testify. I'm just presenting to you this figure from the document sent by the chief of civilian protection in Srebrenica. And he wrote in this document that the total number of population is 36.000. And I also showed you the previous document where he said, Present to international organisations that we have 45.000 people here. So they were deliberately deceiving you. The difference between the actual number of them and the figure they presented to others was 10.000. Now, I am asking you, would they be presenting a much higher figure in order to receive more food?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already said that the UN was working on the figure that we had given, that of 42.000. Not the 45 that was -- that you have shown us here, not the 36 that you are calling actual. We were using the figure of 42. So for the other figures, how they got lower, how the others got it higher, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything. I'm just questioning you on the basis of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask the Trial Chamber if both this and the previous document can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The two documents will be marked for identification, but not pending translation but on another reason. This witness was not able to comment anything of the content of these two documents. One moment, Mr. Tolimir. We need the numbers first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D284 will be Exhibit D116, marked for identification. 65 ter 1D285 will be Exhibit D117, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This representative for civilian affairs in this last table at the bottom, the last box but one, said that there were 11.495 residents aged between 18 and 60. My question is, do you consider these to be military-aged population, those aged between 18 and 60?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, where is that figure? I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There are two tables. We are not looking at the first one, we are now looking at a second one, table 2, where it says "Age and gender structure," and there are three rows in it. Now, the last two columns are people aged 18 to 60, 11.495. Are people 18 to 60 years old considered to be military age? And this is a table that suggests what the actual figures were to the Trial Chamber. This is marked with a cross below the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Be patient with the witness. The witness wanted to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I go ahead? Your Honour, it depends on what you mean by "fighting age" because if this figure between the ages of 18 and 60 is what is considered a fighting age in a certain country, it may not be the same in another country. Furthermore, these people you may not know about them, maybe they are not capable in terms of -- they could be disabled, some of them could be disabled. Some of them maybe do not have fingers which they can use, you know, to trigger -- to use the trigger. Others could be maybe even not interested in fighting. Others, you know, after hitting the age of 50, 55, sometimes you become unable to fight. So it really depends on how a person really is. So you cannot go directly and say the 11.495 are of the fighting age, and therefore maybe deduce that they were actually, you know, soldiers. That cannot be the case. Because even some of these maybe were injured before. They could be having that age between 18 and 60 but they could have been injured. So there are so many other factors that have got to be considered, not just the age between 18 and 60. After all, some of them could be, I don't know because I cannot understand what is written here, some of them could be women. I don't know. And women are not known to be used very well in combat. So this figure is not a direct figure to use that maybe, you know, these are soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Women are shown in a separate box, but this M stands for men and you see the figure of 11.495. The women are not represented in the table. But it doesn't really matter, let's go on. Where you discharged your duties in Srebrenica, did people volunteer to join the army or were they mobilised by the command or the authorities on the ground? What was the principle that was in place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that is a question which is a bit difficult to answer because we never participated in any recruitment of soldiers. In the first place, we did not notice any recruitment. Second, we were not involved if there was any recruitment of soldiers. Whether it was voluntary or otherwise, we were not involved at all. Thirdly, if we could have noticed of any recruitment, we definitely could have reported about it. So we did not notice any, whether voluntary or by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not actually ask about mobilisation. I may have been interpreted wrongly. I asked about the principle of voluntarily joining the army, but I understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you do, that is okay. Because whether voluntary or by force, really we did not get involved in anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I wouldn't even ask you that unless you yourself mentioned that that reason had to be taken into account when calculating the numbers. Since you had an insight into the humanitarian situation which can be seen in your statement as well as in the transcript in the Popovic case where on page 19194, lines 21 through line 25, on the following pages speak about the humanitarian situation. And you say, and I quote: "The situation with the food was still a great concern for our staff, and that's what we did every Sunday. That's what we did every week. We provided weekly reports on food, not only in Srebrenica," and so on and so forth, which means that you did look after that issue and that you reported back to your superiors about that. My question to you is this: What information did you use to arrive at the data that you submitted in your daily and weekly reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I request you show me the document that you just read because you have it, maybe it can be put here so I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is not a document. This is a transcript, a transcript from a trial, and I told you that it was page 19194, line 21, to 19195, line 5, and this is what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can repeat if necessary, if not, then the witness has the transcript to peruse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, don't repeat. It is an exhibit because we received it. It is P950. And perhaps that can be shown to the witness. It is already on the screen. Thank you. Line 21 through the next page, line --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19194. 19194, line 21, to 19195, line 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I doubt if this is the right page number. There's nothing in it you were asking for. Now we have another page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you now see what you said from line 21 onwards? This is your answer. From line 21 where your answer starts. You can read it if you need to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question Mr. Tolimir put to the witness was: What information did you use to arrive at the data that you submitted in your daily and weekly reports? Could you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, the food situation in the enclave, as I had said earlier, was of serious concern to everybody, and especially in the UN system. And we were doing weekly food assessment of the whole enclave, and as reported here, not just the village of Srebrenica. It was everywhere. But Srebrenica town itself is the one that was guiding us mostly because that is where they had a bigger market of foodstuffs and everything else. So we would go there, see what is available in the market, and the prices. That would give us a guide on how the situation is. Is it very desperate, is it okay at whatever time, or how is the situation in the enclave? It would just give an indicator. And then we would use the same report to send to the UN headquarters so they can know what is happening there. One thing to note is that these food reports also helped us understand the dynamics in the food procurement, in terms of movement to and from Zepa, because when you find when food came from those other areas like Zepa, the prices went down because at least there was enough supply. The other source of food was from UNHCR, and when the convoys brought the food inside the enclave, part of what these individuals were given, they could make sure that they don't use everything and part of it they sell so that they can also buy other necessities that they were not being provided for by the UNHCR or any other UN agency. Here we are talking about issues like, you know, they could buy toothpaste, soap, and everything else that they were not being provided. So they would sell part of what they have gotten from UNHCR to do that. So in summary, the weekly food assessment was always done by us. We used to do it. And except when there was a problem like, you know, the fall -- during the fall of the enclave, there we could not be able to do a proper assessment, but at other times we used to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you answer my next question, please. Did you find food from humanitarian convoys on the food stalls in the market in Srebrenica and was there food that arrived in Srebrenica from other sources as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could find some in the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that foodstuffs arrived in other ways across the separation lines, and if that was the case, do you know how it arrived, apart from being brought in by humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll not get tired repeating what I've already said, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I appreciate that Colonel Kingori may not be getting tired of repeating what he has said, but maybe the interpreters are, maybe the record is. Colonel Kingori just described, about 20 lines up, how food was coming in from Zepa sometimes, how some of that food made it into the market, how some of the people in Srebrenica managed to save a little bit of their UNHCR food to sell for other necessities like toothpaste. This witness gave a very detailed answer and now General Tolimir is repeating the same questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Thayer, you repeated some of this answer again, but focus on another topic. You have received an answer and go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the last four minutes. No discussion, please. Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I did not ask about people selling part of the supplies that they had received. I asked the witness whether foodstuffs arrived in Srebrenica in other ways to be sold on the market. In other words, was the humanitarian convoy supply the only way people obtained food at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you received this answer. Page 75, line 19 through line 21. Page 76. Please go ahead, and I mean ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. However, if you put that answer in a broader context, then that answer is not an answer to my question, and it's not clear in any case. In other words, whether there was food in Zepa, if it was for sale in Srebrenica, was the food supplied by the Serbs? There must have been other ways if it did not arrive only through humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR in any way participate in the distribution of the humanitarian aid to the population of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, UNPROFOR was not mandated to supply food to the enclave as such, but they were to provide security for the convoys but for the DutchBat, and especially now we are talking about DutchBat because it was the one that was in that place at that particular moment, was not getting food to go and supply to the residents of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was it who distributed food and controlled the distribution thereof? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The food was being distributed by other agencies, like UNHCR, and I think there were other -- several other organisations which were providing food and medical care, medical supplies, and other reliefs. So there were several other agencies working there, and I mentioned UNHCR, IOM, MSF, and all the others that were working there. So those are the ones who were helping the people inside the enclave. But specifically for UNPROFOR to get food to go and distribute, really that was not normal. That does not mean that if a company is in a certain location and they have some surplus food, they cannot be able to give maybe an individual something they got, whoever is there, some kind of food or something they got. But that is not distribution, that is just giving somebody something that maybe you have to spare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have reached the time for the break for today. Mr. Tolimir, are you able to indicate how many more hours you need for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's very difficult for me to say in view of the lengthy answers provided by this witness. My questions tend to be much shorter than the answer, so it is not very easy for me to give that assessment based on my questions alone. I've not achieved much today. I don't know what is going to happen tomorrow. Please tell me how much more time I have left and then I'll try to ask focused questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think there were two reasons today that perhaps the progress was not as you expected for your own purposes. It's not only that indeed this witness is providing everybody with detailed answers, which takes some time. On the other hand, if you don't repeat every question three times, you save time for the next questions. You will have realised that this Chamber -- it's not the procedure of this Chamber to limit the time for the examination. It is up it to you to indicate how much time you need. At the moment the Chamber is open to both parties for an extension of time indicated earlier. You will have realised that, and we don't want to change this way of procedure because I think it's the best way in the interest of justice. But you should be aware of the time used by your questioning and the many repetitions. That is my request. Perhaps you can provide us with your estimation tomorrow morning. We have to adjourn now. This estimation is important for the purpose of the Prosecution. They have to call and prepare the next witness and their scheduling of all witnesses of this and the next month. That's the reason why I'm asking you. Sir, I'm very sorry, we have to continue your examination tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
